citations.quote: Dept. Electronics Engineering, Technical University of Catalonia-UPC BarcelonaTech, Spain.

This paper presents one such design-oriented tool that can evaluate these autonomous organization schemes—potentially for large-scale and highly heterogeneous scenarios with dynamic contexts and multiple time-scales—and illustrates its usage in the evaluation of an autonomous nano-satellite swarm that collectively optimizes revisit times.

Characterized by the limiting resource capacities of this class of spacecraft (e.g. low power generation and communication bandwidths), densely populated nano-satellite swarms or constellations are seen to require novel operational concepts grounded on autonomy in order to deliver their expected benefits and ultimately make these systems feasible [8].

In this sense, this paper proposes a design-oriented framework (Fig. 1) aimed at addressing these needs, and illustrates its application for an autonomous, self-organizing scheme for nano-satellite swarms. Thus, the objectives of the design-oriented framework presented herein are three-fold: to allow the modelling of the system and simulate its performance; to conceive and implement autonomous operation schemes; and to verify their resulting qualitative aspects and limitations in order to identify and address possible design flaws.

A swarm of EO nano-satellites can be described generically as a system composed of multiple independent agents that capture information of their environment. The motion of these agents is determined by their orbital trajectories. In this work, orbital parameters are assumed to be fixed and predictable, as is the case of most small spacecraft (which tend to lack the ability to perform orbital maneuvers). This simplifies the modelling of the system, albeit makes the problem slightly less generic. Figure 2 depicts the proposed modelling of the system in UML.

EO systems, and especially distributed satellite systems, are often designed to provide data with a given spatial and spectral resolutions, a maximum temporal resolution (i.e. time between two consecutive observations of the same spot, the so-called "revisit time"), and a maximum latency (i.e. the delay between the capturing of data and its reception).

Another determining characteristic is their limited capacity to generate and store energy. When satellite agents enable their observation device (i.e. instrument) they shall inflict a consumption of energy and data storage. Therefore, agents will need to optimize the collection of data while minimizing the resources spent therein. That is to say that their autonomous operations scheme will ultimately solve a scheduling problem subject to resource constraints.

Their state is represented with their remaining resource capacities (e.g. energy and data storage) and position and velocity vectors. Both energy and storage are modelled as Cumulative Resource capacities that do not return to their initial capacity after a consumption rate is removed. Satellite motion is encapsulated in a trajectory model that implements a Keplerian Orbit Propagator. Satellites can exchange information when another agent is within their communication ranges. However, exchange of information can only happen if both agents have enough energy to enable their emulated links.

Agents that have higher computational capabilities (i.e. memory, processing time) will tessellate their Environment Models with smaller cells, whereas satellites that present constraints in memory or processing power, may reduce the number of cells to the minimum. This also emulates the fact that true environment information can never be fully grasped and will always be approximated during the reasoning processes of agents.
The proposed framework implements the aforementioned multi-agent system and complements it with tools that allow the generation and visualization of system metrics and state.

Currently, the characterization of performance is based on two EO metrics, namely, revisit time and coverage, as well as a figure that shows agent's geographical overlapping during simultaneous captures.

In order to verify the modelling approach as well as to test the characterization framework, this paper provides a preliminary collective mission planning scheme that enables autonomous operations and tries to optimize performance and resource utilization. This preliminary organization scheme is grounded on a two-tiered decisional process, implemented as part of the agent's behavior and reasoning capabilities. The low-level process solves a local planning problem, whereas the upper tier implements an activity exchange policy among the agents. In this preliminary version, all agents are assumed to have the same behavior and computation capabilities, although their instrument and communications link present different resource demands and characteristics (e.g. link range and instrument area).

The planning of activities is designed as a scheduling process based on evolutionary heuristics. In particular, the current version of this autonomous operational scheme implements a Genetic Algorithm Scheduler (GAs) that maximizes the objective function in (3), subject to resource constraints [10]:

Each activity defines a consumption rate $ r_{k} $ for each resource k of capacity $ C_{k} $ . The generation of potential activities is carried out based on a function $ p_{\mathcal{E}}(x,y)\in[0,1] $ that computes a payoff figure for each observable point in the trajectory of an agent.

The analysis has focused on two indicators (Fig. 4): system performance and efficiency. The former is represented as the normalized revisit time (where 0 means that the system has not achieved its target performance). The latter indicator, efficiency, is studied with the number of overlapped observations in any given location of the environment. Both indicators have allowed to detect design flaws and incorrect behavior when the system was emulated for a swarm size of 5 and 10 nano-satellites.
Series labeled with "best" correspond to the ficticious value that would be obtained if agent instruments would be enabled constantly (which we know is not possible given power resource constraints).

Although the system would be able to maintain target revisit time, there is a period of time (i.e. $ 3 5 0 0 < t < 4 2 0 0 $ ) where agents repeatedly miss a certain geographical area and yield unexpected performance. Likewise, their revisit time exceeds the target one during most of the time, suggesting that their ability to optimize resource utilization globally can be improved.

The second analysis (Fig. 4b) reveals that the system is slightly inefficient. The number of overlapped measurements of some point in the surface of the Earth has been repeatedly equal or greater than 1. This suggests a lack of coordination between agents and stresses the need to improve the autonomous operational scheme.

The presented framework allowed to characterize an autonomous operational scheme and to identify areas of the design that can benefit from improvements. Likewise, this framework can also be used to perform comprehensive benchmark and trade-off analysis, where multiple different operational schemes can be assessed and compared.

Thus, the uniqueness of the presented characterization framework does not lie in its ability to simulate a distributed and decentralized agent-based system but to explore multiple of their instances, as well as to facilitate both a quantitative and qualitative evaluation of the design [11].
